question.prompt:
Arjun and Beth play a game in which they take turns removing one brick or two adjacent bricks from one “wall” among a set of several walls of bricks, with gaps possibly creating new walls. The walls are one brick tall. For example, a set of walls of sizes \(4\) and \(2\) can be changed into any of the following by one move: \((3,2),\) \(\ (2,1,2),\) \(\ (4),\) \(\ (4,1),\) \(\ (2,2),\) or \((1,1,2).\)

[Figure 1](figures/2021_AMC_12B_Q22_question_fig1.svg)

Arjun plays first, and the player who removes the last brick wins. For which starting configuration is there a strategy that guarantees a win for Beth?

solutions.explanation:
A useful position to leave your opponent is one whose walls can be paired by equal length. Whenever your opponent moves in one wall, copy that removal in its partner. If the removal splits a wall, pair each resulting piece with its copy. This restores equal pairs after every reply. Your reply is always available because the partner wall was untouched, and the number of bricks strictly decreases. Consequently, you take the last brick.

Wall order and orientation do not affect the available moves, so we may list lengths in any order. We first show that \(T=(3,2,1)\) is another position from which the player to move loses. Every possible first move produces one of the positions on the left below. The arrow gives a legal reply that leaves paired walls:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(2,2,1)&\longrightarrow(2,2),\\
(2,1,1,1)&\longrightarrow(1,1,1,1),\\
(2,1,1)&\longrightarrow(1,1),\\
(3,1,1)&\longrightarrow(1,1,1,1),\\
(3,1)&\longrightarrow(1,1),\\
(3,2)&\longrightarrow(2,2).
\end{aligned}
\]
These cases are exhaustive: the 3-wall can become \(2\), \((1,1)\), or \(1\); the 2-wall can become \(1\) or disappear; and the 1-wall can disappear. For example, the fourth reply removes the middle brick of the 3-wall. After any of these replies, the pairing strategy wins. Thus \(T\) is losing for the player to move.

Now consider choice B, \((6,2,1)\), and write \(K=(2,2,1,1)\), a paired position. Removing one brick from the 6-wall leaves \(5\), \((4,1)\), or \((3,2)\), up to reflection. Removing two adjacent bricks leaves \(4\), \((3,1)\), or \((2,2)\). Together with the three possible changes to the shorter walls, these give all nine positions Arjun can leave. Beth can reply as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(5,2,1)&\longrightarrow K,\\
(4,2,1,1)&\longrightarrow K,\\
(3,2,2,1)&\longrightarrow K,\\
(4,2,1)&\longrightarrow K,\\
(3,2,1,1)&\longrightarrow K,\\
(2,2,2,1)&\longrightarrow K,\\
(6,1,1)&\longrightarrow K,\\
(6,1)&\longrightarrow T,\\
(6,2)&\longrightarrow T.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the first six rows, Beth changes a wall by \(5\to(2,1)\), \(4\to2\), \(3\to1\), \(4\to(2,1)\), \(3\to2\), or \(2\to1\), respectively. The two splits use interior removals; the other four use end removals. For the last three rows, number the bricks of the 6-wall from one end. Beth removes bricks \(3,4\), brick \(3\), or bricks \(2,3\), respectively. Every reply therefore leaves Arjun a position already proved losing, so Beth can guarantee a win from B.

For completeness, Arjun can win from every other choice by making paired walls on his first turn:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{A}:\ (6,1,1)&\longrightarrow(2,2,1,1),\\
\mathrm{C}:\ (6,2,2)&\longrightarrow(2,2,2,2),\\
\mathrm{D}:\ (6,3,1)&\longrightarrow(3,3,1,1),\\
\mathrm{E}:\ (6,3,2)&\longrightarrow(3,3,2,2).
\end{aligned}
\]
In the 6-wall, these moves remove bricks \(3,4\) for A and C, bricks \(2,3\) for D, and brick \(3\) for E. Arjun then copies Beth's moves in the paired walls. Hence the unique requested configuration is \(\boxed{(6,2,1)}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
solutions.title: Pair equal walls and check the exceptional positions
